Hi Mark. Last class you kept a conversation going with a tiny question. Today you look back at the trip, and there are two things you can do. You can regret, or you can guess. You already know should have and could have from an earlier lesson. I should have packed a raincoat. We could have seen Mount Fuji. Today there is something new. Needn't have means you did something, and it was not necessary. We needn't have taken so much cash. Didn't need to usually means it was not necessary, so you did not do it. We didn't need to buy tickets, because the museum was free. Now the guesses. When you are almost sure something happened, say must have. You must have been exhausted after that flight. When you are almost sure it did not happen, say can't have. It can't have been cheap. And when you do not know, say might have. Now the traps. Should have sounds like should of in fast speech, but it is always have. The opposite of must have is can't have, never mustn't have, because mustn't is for rules. And needn't have is not the same as didn't need to. Before class, write your three biggest travel regrets, and one thing you needn't have done.

Welcome back to the show. This week I want to talk about my first trip to Japan, because I made almost every mistake you can make. First, I booked everything at the last minute, so I paid double for the hotel. I should have booked three months earlier. Second, I bought a rail pass for the whole week, and I only used it twice. I needn't have spent all that money. Third, and this one still hurts, there was a clear morning when we could have gone up to see Mount Fuji. We stayed in bed instead, and it rained for the rest of the trip. I could kick myself. A listener wrote to me last week and said, you must have been very tired, then. Maybe. But I think I just took the trip for granted. I thought there would be another chance. So here is my advice. Plan the big things early, spend less on the things you might not use, and when a once-in-a-lifetime moment appears, get out of bed. Thanks for listening.

Before the trip, I booked everything at the last minute, so I paid double. I should have booked three months earlier. At the station, I bought a rail pass for the whole week, but I only used it twice, so I needn't have spent that money. On the fourth morning, the sky was clear, and we could have gone to see Mount Fuji, but we stayed in bed. After that, it rained every day, and I could kick myself. At the end, I realized I had taken the whole trip for granted. Lesson learned.
